_comment: Frame time is a property of a machine, not of the build: an M4's ms/frame means nothing on a CI runner's software renderer, so there is no single global number here, only one block per machine_tag (see bench.c's bench_finish for how the tag is built and prof.h for what frame_ms_median is a median of). A machine_tag that is not a key below has no baseline yet, and tools/bench_check.py treats that as 'nothing to compare against' rather than a pass or a fail on its own -- pass --allow-missing-baseline to let a run with no baseline through anyway (CI does this today). The rule going forward: the same commit that adds or changes a CI job's bench step must also add that runner's tag here, learned from that job's own first green run, so the tolerance check actually gates something instead of quietly no-op'ing forever. Each path also records the draw and triangle counts it was taken at, and bench_check.py shouts when those have moved more than 5%: a baseline is a number about a SCENE as much as about a build, so a level content change (new props, a different scatter, a decimated model) invalidates it and the right response is to re-take it in the same commit, not to argue with the frame time. Re-take it with: ./build/bin/goonstein --bench out.json --volume 0, several times, and keep the lowest median per path -- noise only ever adds time.

metal/macOS/10._note: The dev machine, an M4 laptop. These are not the fastest this machine has produced -- that is 1.740 / 1.689 / 2.017 / 1.818 and it is what README quotes -- but the worst that the gate's OWN procedure (the lowest median of three runs) produced across five runs of an unchanged tree. A baseline has to be reachable by the check that reads it, or the check fails on a good day and everyone learns to ignore it.

metal/macOS/3._note: A GitHub-hosted macOS runner: three shared cores and a shared GPU. Numbers learned from the `Perf bench (macOS)` job's own bench.json, lowest median of its three runs.
